Executive Summary

Introduction

In this report, we examine the association between hospital bed occupancy levels and the propensity of ED clinicians to order tests. This is the second of two NHSE-commissioned reports that examine the impact of the growth in diagnostic testing on urgent and emergency care services.

Work on the first phase of this project, detailed in Growth in Diagnostic Testing and Its Impact on Emergency Departments (Strategy Unit, 2025), indicated that, between 2019/20 and 2023/24, the casemix-adjusted odds of a patient receiving a test increased for most test types. Moreover, having received a test, the casemix-adjusted odds that a patient would be admitted fell.

The analysis we present here examines whether the increased odds of testing and decreased odds of admission are causally (note: this was in the original “Further Research” text - don’t know if we’re now suggesting we can do this) related / are associated. One theory is that, by testing more, clinicians are able to rule out conditions that would otherwise involve admission. It is unclear, however, if clinical practice in EDs is leading this change, or if practice is responding to changes in the operational context (in particular, to the reduced availability of beds).

We investigate this this issue by developing regression models to examine whether, and the extent to which, the odds of a patient receiving a test varies with bed occupancy levels. Significant evidence of a “bed occupancy” effect would indicate that increased testing may be, in part, driven by reduced bed availability.

This report takes the form of a standard scientific paper: we continue with details of the method used, before presenting the Results and Discussion sections.

Method

This analysis covers ED attendances at major (Type 1) emergency departments. For ED attendance data, we relied on the SUS ECDS, whilst for a provider’s bed occupancy levels we used the SUS APC data set. These are both high-quality, patient-level sources. However, we observed considerable variation in recording practices, both across the population of provider trusts and over time. If overlooked, this variation would adversely affect both the reliability and validity of our results.

The use of provider sampling

To increase the chances that our findings would be both valid and reliable, we conducted the analysis on data from a sample of 25 providers. This sample was non-random: we included a provider in the sample if the quality of their data submissions met our requirements.

Whilst sampling should improve the reliability and validity of our results, we can only make general statements about the association between testing thresholds and bed occupancy if our sample of providers is representative of the population of providers. That is to say that, on aggregate, the providers in our sample should have similar characteristics to those in our population.

There is a trade-off to be made here. The larger our sample of providers, the more likely it is to be representative of the population of providers. However, the larger we make our sample, the more we compromise on data quality, which will likely to decrease the reliability of our results.

Details of our approach to this trade-off, as well as our data quality criteria, sampling methods, and the measures of representation, can be found in Section 6.

Excluded attendances

For providers within our sample, the analyses covers all unplanned attendances of persons with an English postcode, with some exceptions: We excluded cases were a person left the ED before being treated, and persons streamed to other care services. In addition, we excluded cases where the patient died during an attendance and those where the patient was found to be dead on arrival at the ED.

Data preparation

Approximately 5.5% of the 2.5 million records in our sample had missing values in one or more key field. (Our “key fields” are given in Section 6.) As our chosen model type will not accept missing values, we opted to delete these records. This involved the assumption that these values are missing at random.

Production of the bed occupancy variable involved several steps. To begin with, we calculated the total number of patients in hospital beds (a proxy for overall hospital busyness) at each of the providers in our sample, for every hour in 2023/24. For this, we required admission and discharge times provided in the SUS APC data set.

Whilst the completeness of admission and discharge times in our sample was high (due to our data quality thresholds), we developed a kNN-based algorithm to impute times for (<1%) records without these values. This was necessary since missing admission or discharge times - for even a single patient - would invalidate a provider’s occupancy count indefinitely. Within provider, admission method, and day of the week groups, the kNN algorithm identified the record that was most similar (k =1) to the record with the missing value, based on a specified combination of admission time or discharge time (where valid), and length of stay. This combination was dependent on the pattern of missingness and whether the admission was a “same-day” admission.

In order to move from hourly counts of beds occupied within each provider, to a relative occupancy level that could be compared across providers and times, we scaled the occupancy at a specific hour, weekday, and provider to the mean occupancy for that hour, weekday, and provider. This scaled occupancy value was our variable of interest.

We then linked these provider-level occupancy values to patient-level ED attendance records, such that an attendance record would show the provider’s occupancy at a patient’s time of arrival. A sensitivity analysis, given in Section 7 shows that the results would change little if we were to use a provider’s occupancy at the midpoint between a patient’s time of arrival and their departure.

Model specification

Moving from data preparation to the modelling stage, we built 32 distinct models to predict casemix-adjusted odds-of-test ratios for 32 (of 49) test types that appear in the EC data set. These 32 tests account for over 99% of all tests recorded in EDs.

We performed logistic regressions using generalised additive models (GAMs) with mixed-effects. All 32 models were specified in the same way, with the only difference being the binary dependent variable (whether the given test was carried out). Our fixed effects included several time-related variables to control for season, weekday, and hour of arrival, as well as the variable of interest: scaled occupancy level at time of arrival. We included variables to adjust for casemix (as far as possible), namely: age (as a spline-based smooth) interacting with sex; a re-engineered chief complaint variable; acuity; arrival mode; and referral source.

(It is important to note that the chief complaint and acuity variables are recorded as part of an initial assessement (NHSE, 2022). They are therefore akin to presentation codes. Whilst the diagnosis codes may give greater detail about a patient’s condition (and better allow us to control for casemix), diagnosis is often a causal consequence of testing and it would be therefore inappropriate to use diagnosis-related information to predict whether a patient receives a given test.)

We treated the provider variable as a random effect. This allowed us to control for factors that vary, at random, across providers. Moreover, the values produced by this random effect can be thought of as sample values from a larger population of values. As the providers in our data set were, in fact, a sample of all providers, this approach suits our case well.

We developed preliminary models, in which the scaled occupancy values were apportioned to quintiles, to satisfy ourselves that the relationship between odds of test and occupancy level was broadly linear.

Our final models were run on the same random sub-sample of 1 million attendance records (from a possible 2.3 million).

Characteristics of patients in the study

Selected characteristics of the patients covered by our analysis data set are shown in Table 1.

The occupancy variable

As detailed in the Methods section, we scaled a provider’s occupancy at a specific hour, weekday, to the mean occupancy for that hour and weekday, at that provider. This scaled occupancy value was our variable of interest. Figure 1 and Figure 2 show distributions of this variable by hour and day of the week, and by provider. Distributions are largely centred on 1 - as expected. We note bimodal distributions for some providers.

  • Occupancy by day of week, and time of day
  • Occupancy by provider

Occupancy and testing thresholds

Figure 3 suggests that the association between hospital bed occupancy levels and the propensity of ED clinicians to order tests varies considerably by test type.

Patients were significantly more likely to receive imaging procedures when bed occupancy levels were 5% higher than average (given the day of the week and the hour of the day). Within imaging, the greatest effect was seen for MRI. Here, a patient was 8% more likely to receive a scan when the hospital was busier than average

The models give odds ratios - interpreted as a one unit increase in scaled occupancy.

Here’s my attempt to articulate my reflections on / understanding (or lack of it) of this section:

We are speculating that, when occupancy is high, clinicians are more likely to test in order to send patients home rather than admit. The key part is that bed numbers are limited. (Our titular, “lack of available beds”).

However, if we look only at bed occupancy numbers in this section, we get no sense of constraint (unless we make the assumption that numbers of beds available haven’t changed- which we probably shouldn’t do: While overnight bed occupancy has increased by ~10% (according to KH03), so has the number of beds available. It’s true that we used occupancy counts to derive the variable of interest in our model. But the scaling does (to me) imply some (necessary) sense of constraint, as we have:

  1. Distrubutions (normal-ish due to central limit theorem, or close relation of (?))- so it’s highly unlikely that we’ll see values exceeding a certain number). and
  1. Related - a mean /expected / reference level.

Discussion

Summary of Results…

Limitations

The findings of this analysis are based on a sample of 25 providers (of 121 providers active submitting returns in every month of the year). As the 25 providers were chosen on the basis of their data quality, this constitutes a non-random sample of providers. Study conclusions drawn from non-random samples are at higher risk of bias. As noted in Section 3.0.1, we attempted to mitigate the risk of bias by confirming that the sample was generally representative of the population of providers in various dimensions. It is, however, possible that we unknowingly omitted important dimensions of representation for this particular question, and that our findings are less generalisable than we suggest.

We have labelled our estimates as “casemix-adjusted” as we controlled for a range of variables that might indicate a patient’s need for a test. However, a clinician will order a test based on an array of factors and only some of these will be recorded in data sets. Therefore, as we are unable to control for unrecorded variables, part of the effect that we measured may be due to unobserved case mix factors.

Finally, as noted in the Methods section above, we decided to delete approximately 6% of records from our sample that had missing values for any of the variables used in the model. If these missing values were missing completely at random, this decision will have a limited impact on our results (by reducing our sample size in this way, we may have marginally increased the standard errors around our model coefficients). There is, however, some potential for bias in our results if these missing data were not missing completely at random.

Appendix 1

To carry out this analysis, we required the SUS EC and APC data sets. We looked at the financial year 2023/24, only. We identified 121 providers who recorded data for the entire year. These 121 providers represent the total population of providers that we might have used for our analysis had data quality been universally high.

However, since data quality was highly variable, we conducted the analysis on data from a sample of providers. We included a provider in our sample if, within the:

  • EC data set: they had all three of Der_EC_Investigation_All, Chief_Complaint, and Acuity complete for 90% of records . (Relaxing this requirement to 85% gave us only a few more providers and no improvement in representation.)

  • APC data set: providers recorded admission and discharge times in at least 99% of cases.

We established that 25 providers met both these criteria. These providers are given in Table 3. In the adjacent tab, Table 4 suggests that this sample of 25 providers is generally representative of the population of providers. We note that the sample includes higher proportions of medium-sized providers and providers in the Midlands.

Appendix 2

In the primary analysis, we measured bed occupancy at the time of a patient’s arrival at the ED. We then investigated how this occupancy affected the odds that a patient would receive a test. In this sensitivity analysis, we examine the effect on results if we measure occupancy at the mid-point between the patient’s arrival and departure time.
